person: Captain Second Rank Vasili Arkhipov, chief of staff of the brigade
card: Sixty meters down in the Caribbean, aboard the diesel submarine B-59. One day, 27 October · 6 decisions. There is a nuclear torpedo aboard your submarine.
intro: You are Vasili Aleksandrovich Arkhipov, 36, chief of staff of the 69th Submarine Brigade of the Northern Fleet. On 1 October the brigade’s four Foxtrot-class diesel submarines (B-4, B-36, B-59 and B-130) left Sayda Bay to escort Operation Anadyr on its way to Cuba, and you are aboard one of them, B-59. Her captain is Captain Second Rank Valentin Savitsky; her political officer is Ivan Maslennikov. Each submarine carries 22 torpedoes, one of them with a nuclear warhead. You are not the captain, but as brigade chief of staff you hold the same rank, and you are the only man aboard who can question his decisions. In July 1961 you were executive officer of the nuclear submarine K-19 when her reactor failed. Times are given in fleet time (Q, UTC minus 4 hours).
allyLabel: Trust of the Captain and Crew

AR-00.place: Sayda Bay, Kola Peninsula: the 69th Submarine Brigade’s anchorage
AR-00.title: One Envelope, One Torpedo

map.caption: The 69th Brigade’s four Foxtrot-class submarines left Sayda Bay on 1 October and sailed some 8,000 kilometers to the Sargasso Sea.

AR-00.event: On the night of 30 September, torpedoes were loaded aboard the four submarines. The Northern Fleet headquarters’ after-action report recorded it this way: each boat was loaded with 21 torpedoes with conventional warheads and one torpedo with a nuclear warhead, and preparations for the operation were complete on 30 September.
AR-00.scene: A few hours before sailing, the brigade commander, Captain First Rank Agafonov, and the submarine captains gathered in the staff hut on the pier. Admiral Fokin and Rassokho, the fleet chief of staff, briefed them, and each captain received a top secret envelope, to be opened only after clearing Kola Bay. Only when they open it will they learn that their destination is Mariel in Cuba and their mission is to escort the transports of Operation Anadyr. The conditions for using the nuclear torpedo were passed on by word of mouth, not in writing, and accounts of what was said will later differ. Paragraph 8 of the combat instructions, as the captains remember it, covers only conventional weapons: during the voyage weapons are to be kept at combat readiness; conventional weapons are to be used on the order of the commander-in-chief of the navy, or if the submarine comes under armed attack. As chief of staff, you must decide which of the four submarines to sail in. Captain Savitsky of B-59 has a reputation as able but hot-tempered, and the brigade commander is sailing in B-4.

voices.text: Paragraph 8 of the combat instructions for the commanders read as follows: during the voyage, weapons are to be kept at combat readiness; conventional weapons are to be used on the order of the commander-in-chief of the navy, or in the event of an armed attack on the submarine. So whether to use weapons depended on how one read the situation. Was cannon fire from an aircraft an armed attack, or not?

voices.who: Nikolai Shumkov (captain of B-130, recalling later)
voices.text: A security officer for the special weapon sails with us. He made it absolutely clear that the nuclear torpedo could not be armed without permission from headquarters. Even if the captain gives the order, there is one more step in the procedure.

choices.text: Follow the custom that the chief of staff sails in a different boat from the brigade commander, and board B-59: Captain Savitsky needs his chief of staff beside him
choices.why: A hot-tempered captain needs a man of equal rank at his side
choices.after: You climbed down B-59’s ladder. Seventy-eight crew, three diesels, the batteries, and the special weapon in torpedo tube No. 1. At 4 a.m. on 1 October the four boats left Sayda Bay at one-hour intervals.

choices.text: Board B-4 with the brigade commander, concentrating the brigade command post in one boat, and send Savitsky his instructions by radio
choices.why: Command must sit in one place, or there will be confusion
choices.after: The brigade commander shook his head. A chief of staff does not sail in the commander’s own boat, he said; go to Savitsky. You climbed down B-59’s ladder. No one knew what that decision would mean nearly a month later.

note.text: All four Foxtrot-class (Project 641) boats of the 69th Brigade carried one nuclear torpedo each. In October 1962 the US Navy did not know that Soviet diesel submarines carried nuclear weapons; this became known only after Soviet participants revealed it at the 2002 Havana conference. The wording of the envelope puts into documentary form what Dubivko and Arkhipov recalled of its contents (destination Mariel, escort of the transport convoy); the original text has not been released.

telegram.to: Captain Second Rank Savitsky, commanding submarine B-59
telegram.cc: Captain First Rank Agafonov, commanding 69th Submarine Brigade
telegram.subject: To be opened after passing Kola Bay
telegram.text: Operation Anadyr. Destination: Mariel, Cuba. Mission: escort transport convoy and reconnoiter assigned patrol area. / Maintain secrecy on passage. Communications at designated times only. / Use of special weapon per separate instructions.

pressure.title: Which Submarine?
pressure.text: By custom the brigade chief of staff sails in a different boat from the brigade commander, and the commander is sailing in B-4. Captain Savitsky has a reputation as able but hot-tempered, and the conditions for using the nuclear torpedo were given only orally, in the briefings by Admiral Fokin and Rassokho, the fleet chief of staff, so that later accounts of them differ. Paragraph 8 of the combat instructions, as the captains remember it, set conditions only for conventional weapons, and you said later that whether cannon fire from an aircraft counted as an armed attack was up to the man reading the situation. Fifteen months ago, aboard K-19, you were the executive officer standing beside the captain in a submarine whose reactor had burst, and eight of her crew died. Inside a submarine, the only man who can question the captain’s decisions is a chief of staff of equal rank, and tonight decides which submarine that man will be in.
pressure.src: Arkhipov 1997; Northern Fleet report 1962-12; Stage 1 issue 3

AR-01.place: Sargasso Sea, Atlantic: B-59’s control room
AR-01.title: The Assigned Patrol Area
AR-01.clock: About 12 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (10 a.m. Washington time, 24 October)

telegram.to: Commanders of submarines B-4, B-36, B-59 and B-130, 69th Submarine Brigade
telegram.subject: Deployment to assigned areas and reconnaissance
telegram.text: Proceed to assigned patrol areas, deploy and conduct reconnaissance. / American provocations against Cuba and our transports possible. / Full combat readiness. Maintain covert passage.
telegram.sign: Chief of the Main Naval Staff

AR-01.event: On the night of 22 October (2 a.m. on the 23rd in Moscow), President Kennedy revealed the Soviet missiles in Cuba on television and declared a naval quarantine. Moscow knew of the speech but did not call the brigade home. Cables from Moscow, picked up by raising the antenna once every four hours, are swamped by jamming each time transmission begins, so receiving a single order in full takes anywhere from a few hours to a day.
AR-01.scene: Under the red lights of the control room, the radio officer took down the radiogram from Moscow. It orders the boat to an assigned patrol area 300–350 miles from the Bahama Channel. That area lies right across the path where American carrier groups run their anti-submarine patrols. The submarine must stay submerged by day and surface at night to run its diesels through the snorkel and recharge the batteries, and every time it comes up it shows on the radar of American patrol planes. Captain Dubivko of B-36 says he has been ordered to fall back 100 miles from the channel; your boat has had no such word. Captain Savitsky reads the cable twice and looks at you. Go to the patrol area and you will be found; stay away and you disobey orders.

voices.text: The order is to deploy to the assigned area. Whether we’re found is their business; whether we go is ours. Chief of Staff, are there separate instructions from the brigade?

The submarine commanders received an order from the Navy’s central command to deploy to their assigned areas and carry out reconnaissance. The same radiogram warned of possible American provocations against Cuba and our transports. We were to be at full combat readiness and to continue our passage covertly.

choices.text: Enter the patrol area as ordered, but run deep by day and charge only briefly after moonset, betting on putting off discovery
choices.why: The chief of staff’s job is to obey the order while delaying the moment of discovery
choices.after: On 24 October B-59 entered the assigned patrol area. At 10 a.m. that day (Washington time) the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba) came into force. The Soviet transports stopped or turned back short of the blockade line, but no one told the submarines to come home.

choices.text: Treat the order as incomplete because of poor reception, and wait submerged where you are for a confirming cable from the brigade commander
choices.why: You cannot send the boat into mortal danger on half an order heard through jamming
choices.after: You waited a day, but no cable came from the brigade commander. The jamming was not only on Moscow’s side. On 25 October you finally turned the boat toward the assigned area and entered the same waters a day late.

choices.text: Hold the outer edge of the patrol area, taking up a position 100 miles back from the channel as B-36 has, and report that position to the brigade
choices.why: A guess that Dubivko’s order reflects the intent for the whole brigade
choices.after: The report went out, but no answer came. The edge was no safer. The patrol radius of the Randolph carrier group was far wider than the assigned area.

note.text: Of the four boats, B-130 surfaced on the night of 25 October when all three of her diesels broke down, and was found by the Essex carrier group. The Soviet submarines communicated with Moscow at four-hour intervals, and the Northern Fleet report states that jamming delayed the receipt of orders by anywhere from a few hours to a day. The original radiogram has not been released; the text here puts Arkhipov’s 1997 summary into cable form.

map.caption: B-59’s assigned patrol area lay in the Sargasso Sea south of Bermuda, outside the quarantine line.

AR-02.place: Inside the assigned patrol area, submerged at 50 meters
AR-02.title: Batteries
AR-02.clock: About a day of submerged running left on the batteries
AR-02.event: On the night of 25 October B-130 surfaced, and Senior Lieutenant Orlov of the radio intercept team heard from American communications that she was being tracked. That same day Washington let the Soviet tanker Bucharest through the quarantine line without inspection, and Moscow ordered ships still outside the blockade line to stop. None of it reached B-59.
AR-02.scene: The batteries are running down. A Foxtrot must surface every night to charge them with its diesels, and to do that the snorkel has to be raised above the water. But Neptune patrol planes circle in the night sky, and the sonar picks up the splash of sonobuoys dropping into the sea. Surface and you are found; stay down and the batteries die. When the batteries die, the boat can no longer stay submerged at all. It is already over 40°C inside, and the cooling plant, built for Arctic waters, is useless in the tropics. Water is one cup a day, and men have begun to collapse with rashes and exhaustion. Captain Savitsky keeps putting off the charge.

voices.text: Chief of Staff, on what’s left we won’t get through tomorrow’s daylight. We need two hours on the surface tonight. If a patrol plane comes, we’ll just have to break off and go down.

voices.who: Vadim Orlov (head of the radio intercept team, recalling later)
voices.text: B-59’s batteries were discharged to the bottom, and only the emergency lights were on. The temperature in the compartments was 45–50°C, and up to 60°C in the engine compartment. The level of CO2 in the air reached a critical mark, practically deadly for people. One of the duty officers fainted and fell down. Then another one followed, then a third. They were falling like dominoes.

choices.text: Time the gaps between patrol planes and surface briefly, several times, to charge, diving at once whenever sonobuoys fall
choices.why: Dead batteries are a surer end than the risk of discovery
choices.after: After two trips up had added an hour of charging, the sonar picked up a destroyer’s screws. Savitsky ordered a crash dive. The batteries were not even half charged. On the morning of 27 October the destroyers of the Randolph carrier group fixed B-59’s position.

choices.text: Give up on charging, stay submerged at minimum speed, and spend every remaining amp slipping out of the patrol area
choices.why: A reading that staying undiscovered is the heart of the order
choices.after: The boat crept along, and the air grew fouler. On the morning of 27 October, when you heard the destroyers with almost no power left, you had nothing left to run with.

choices.text: Propose to the captain that you surface outright and charge in the open, as B-130 did, reckoning that even if found, a submarine on the high seas will not be sunk
choices.why: Keeping the crew alive comes before staying hidden
choices.after: Savitsky refused. Covert passage was an order, he said, and surfacing as Shumkov had done was for a boat that had broken down. Your proposal did not go into the log, but the next day the same words would come up again.

note.text: Conditions inside the submarines (250 grams of water a day, skin rashes, 40–65°C) come from the recollections of Captain Dubivko of B-36; the 45–60°C aboard B-59 and the men collapsing one after another come from Orlov’s. The US Navy’s anti-submarine operation was part of the quarantine mission. On 24 October Defense Secretary McNamara reported to the ExComm a procedure for signaling Soviet submarines to surface with practice depth charges (PDCs); Moscow was notified of the procedure, but it was never passed on to the submarines.

pressure.title: Between Charging and Discovery
pressure.text: Surface and you are found; stay down and the batteries die. It is over 40°C inside, water is one cup a day, and men have begun to collapse with rashes and exhaustion. Orlov heard over American communications that B-130 had surfaced with all three diesels broken down and been found by the Essex group. Word has not reached this boat that on 24 October McNamara reported a procedure for signaling Soviet submarines to surface with practice depth charges, or that Moscow was told of it. You saw in K-19’s compartments how much a human body can take. Tonight’s question is which to save first, the batteries or the crew.
pressure.src: Orlov 2002; Northern Fleet report 1962-12; FRUS XI d60

AR-03.time: Afternoon (Q time, per US Navy records)
AR-03.place: B-59, submerged at 60 meters, all compartments
AR-03.title: Hammering on an Iron Barrel
AR-03.clock: About 4 hours since the depth charges began; carbon dioxide at the critical level
AR-03.event: That morning a US Air Force U-2 was shot down over Cuba by a Soviet surface-to-air missile, and another U-2, out of Alaska, lost its way and strayed into Soviet airspace. In Washington, Khrushchev’s second letter (the swap for the missiles in Turkey) came in over the radio. You know none of this. B-59’s radio has not heard Moscow for three days.
AR-03.scene: The destroyers Beale and Cony are overhead. Sonar counts the screws of nine ships, and there are several aircraft as well. Practice depth charges the size of hand grenades have begun bursting close to the hull. Orlov wrote that it was like sitting inside an iron barrel while someone outside kept beating on it with a sledgehammer. This is the fourth hour. Only the emergency lights are left; the thermometers read 50°C in the compartments and 60°C in the engine room, and the carbon dioxide reading is off the top of the scale. The officers on watch collapse one after another. The captain zigzags to shake off the pursuit, but on batteries the boat cannot make speed. If you surface, no one knows whether you will be seized, sunk, or whether it is only a signal. This submarine does not know that Moscow has been told of the American procedure for signaling submarines to surface with depth charges.

voices.text: It felt like you were sitting in a metal barrel, which somebody is constantly blasting with a sledgehammer.
Chief of Staff, these aren’t live charges. If they were, the hull would have split open by now. They’re trying to tell us something. What, I don’t know either.
If they want to tell us something, they can send a message instead of throwing depth charges. We’ll zigzag out of it once more. If that doesn’t work, we’ll think again then.

choices.text: Back the captain: stay submerged and keep changing course to shake off the pursuit, holding surfacing in reserve as a last resort
choices.why: As long as the charges are not live, hiding is what the orders call for
choices.after: Two more hours went by. The pursuit did not let go, and more men collapsed. Then a blast unlike any before, much louder, struck the hull.

choices.text: Tell the captain flatly that if you hold out any longer men will die, and demand that you surface at once and proceed on the surface
choices.why: When saving the boat and saving the men part ways, choose the men
choices.after: Savitsky looked at you for a long moment, then ordered the boat to surface. The sonar signal went out and the submarine came up: you had got through that night before the nuclear torpedo was ever mentioned. But on the surface a different kind of danger was waiting.

choices.text: Propose rising to antenna depth to try once more for orders from Moscow: with an order in hand, the captain has less room for discretion
choices.why: A calculation to hand responsibility for the decision to Moscow
choices.after: At antenna depth the radio officer picked up nothing but jamming. Moscow could not be heard, and meanwhile the destroyers closed in. Then a blast unlike any before, much louder, struck the hull.

note.text: The deck logs of the US destroyers Beale (USS Beale) and Cony (USS Cony) record the dropping of practice depth charges. A practice depth charge carries about as much explosive as a hand grenade, and the US Navy had designated it as the signal to surface. The crew of B-59 did not know what the signal meant.

AR-04.place: B-59’s control room, before torpedo tube No. 1
AR-04.title: The Special Weapon
AR-04.event: A bigger blast struck the hull. To Orlov, head of the intercept team, it sounds like a live depth charge. Sixty meters down, there is no telling a practice charge from a live one.
AR-04.scene: Captain Savitsky called for the officer in charge of the nuclear torpedo and ordered the special weapon assembled to combat readiness. His words were these: maybe the war has already started up there, and here we are turning somersaults; we’re going to fire; we will die, but we will sink them all; we will not disgrace the navy. The control room is silent. The torpedo officer looks from the captain to you and back. There are no written conditions for using the nuclear torpedo, and you and the captain hold the same rank. The political officer, Maslennikov, is standing beside you. There is talk that firing requires the agreement of three men, but no document laying that down exists aboard this submarine. What exists is whatever you say at this moment.

voices.who: Valentin Savitsky (captain, as reported by Orlov)
voices.text: Maybe the war has already started up there, and meanwhile this boat is down here turning somersaults. We’re going to fire. We’ll die, but we’ll sink them all. We will not disgrace the navy.
Comrade Captain, we have never received a cable saying the war has begun. Not having received one is not the same as its having begun.
Whether to use weapons depended on how one read the situation. Was cannon fire from an aircraft an armed attack, or not?

choices.text: Oppose arming it: there has been no order to start a war, and the depth charges have not split the hull. Propose sending a sonar signal and surfacing to find out
choices.why: The principle of doing nothing irreversible while you do not know
choices.after: For a while the captain said nothing. Orlov wrote that Savitsky swallowed his anger. After consulting you and Maslennikov, the captain decided to surface. Following the international rules of navigation, the boat sent the surfacing signal by sonar, and the pursuing ships slowed.

choices.text: Back the captain: treat the “armed attack” of paragraph 8 of the combat instructions as having already happened, and approve arming the special weapon and preparing to fire
choices.why: In a sea cut off from orders, the captain’s judgment is the order
choices.after: The torpedo officer went to tube No. 1 with the security officer. Arming it took time, and all that time the depth charges kept coming.

choices.text: Propose attacking the nearest destroyer with a conventional torpedo instead of the nuclear one: meet armed attack with arms, but with a weapon that leaves a way back
choices.why: A compromise that avoids catastrophe without crushing the captain’s fury
choices.after: Savitsky looked at you a moment, then nodded. Conventional torpedoes were loaded into tubes No. 2 and No. 3. Sonar picked up the nearest screws. It was the destroyer Cony.

note.text: Savitsky’s words in this scene rest on Orlov’s recollections, published in 2002. The testimony of Ketov, captain of B-4, and other submarine commanders differs somewhat: after surfacing, startled on the bridge by searchlights and cannon fire, the captain shouted for a crash dive and for torpedo No. 1 to be readied, but could not get below because the ladder was blocked; Arkhipov, who stayed on the bridge and saw that the Americans were signaling, called him back. In no account did an order to arm the torpedo actually reach the torpedo officer. The “three-officer rule” is widely repeated, but nothing in the documents confirms it.
note.src: Orlov 2002; NSA 2022 commentary (Ketov testimony); Stage 1 issue 3

pressure.title: Two Men of Equal Rank
pressure.text: As Orlov later reported them, the captain’s words were that the war might already have begun up there, that he would fire, that they would die but sink them all, and that he would not disgrace the navy. There are no written conditions for using the nuclear torpedo; you and the captain hold the same rank, and the political officer is standing beside you. It is widely said that the torpedo could be fired only if three men agreed, the captain, the political officer and the chief of staff, but historians note that the rule rests not on documents but only on later testimony. Orlov recalled that the captain decided to surface after talking it over with you and Maslennikov; Ketov’s story is that the captain, startled on the bridge by searchlights and cannon fire, shouted for a crash dive and for a torpedo to be readied, was blocked on the ladder, and was called back by you. In no account did an order to arm the torpedo actually reach the torpedo officer. Everything comes down to what the chief of staff says to the captain at this moment, and whether the captain listens.
pressure.src: Orlov 2002; NSA 2022 commentary; Arkhipov 1997; Stage 1 issue 3

AR-05.title: Searchlights
AR-05.clock: About 6 hours needed to charge the batteries
AR-05.event: The submarine surfaced. On the night sea were the carrier Randolph, nine destroyers, four Neptune patrol planes and three Trackers. When the hatch opened, the hot night air felt cool after the heat of the compartments.
AR-05.scene: The moment you and the captain stepped onto the bridge, an aircraft passed 20 meters overhead and switched on a searchlight. No one on the bridge could see. Then came the sound of cannon. Twelve low passes, about 300 rounds; the destroyers close to 20–50 meters, train their guns on you and shout something through loudspeakers. For the one to three seconds you are blind, you cannot tell whether this is fire or a threat. It is the moment when the captain can shout for a crash dive, and if you dive, the nuclear torpedo will come up again. When your sight returns, you see the rounds passing beside and ahead of the submarine and falling into the sea. The Americans are firing, but not hitting. Someone on the bridge has to say what that means.

voices.text: After the first burst of cannon fire from the aircraft, the commander could have ordered a crash dive instinctively, without thinking. And then, once submerged, the question of whether the plane had fired at the submarine or around it would not have entered anyone’s head. That is war. But one to three seconds before the firing, the plane passing over the bridge switched on a powerful searchlight, and the people on the bridge were blinded by a light so strong it hurt their eyes. It was a shock. The commander was physically unable to give any order. When, after blinking again and again, we could see once more, it became clear that the plane was firing past the side of the boat, ahead of it and astern.
If that’s a warning, it’s too close for a warning. One stray round and the bridge is gone. Wouldn’t it be better to go down and settle this?

choices.text: Block any order until your eyes recover; once you have seen the fire is passing wide of the boat, keep charging on the surface and signal for the provocation to stop
choices.why: Hold on through those one to three seconds, and you can tell war from a signal
choices.after: The rounds fell wide of the submarine. The destroyers kept their distance. The diesels started, and the air inside the boat changed. The charging went on all night.

choices.text: Order a crash dive to escape the fire, and decide once submerged whether to answer with torpedo No. 1 (nuclear)
choices.why: The instinct that deciding underwater beats being shot dead on the bridge
choices.after: The submarine went back under. The batteries were almost empty, and, just as Arkhipov later said, underwater no one asked whether the plane had fired at the submarine or beside it. Conventional torpedoes were loaded into the tubes.

note.text: The Northern Fleet report states that aircraft and helicopters from the Randolph made 12 passes at altitudes of 20–100 meters, firing about 300 rounds, and that destroyers closed to 20–50 meters with their guns trained on the boat. US Navy records state that B-59 surfaced and charged her batteries that night. What signal the submarine sent is not recorded in the Northern Fleet report or in Arkhipov’s presentation, so it is left out here.

pressure.title: One to Three Seconds Blind
pressure.text: An aircraft passes over the bridge and switches on a searchlight, and one to three seconds later its cannon opens up. Twelve low passes, about 300 rounds; the destroyers close to between 20 and 50 meters and train their guns on you. You said later that if the captain had instinctively ordered a crash dive after the first burst, no one, once submerged, would have asked whether the plane had fired at the submarine or around it, and that this would have been war. But the searchlight blinded the captain so that he could not give an order, and when his sight returned he could see the rounds passing beside and ahead of the boat. In those few seconds, whatever is said first on the bridge becomes the order. After your return, Vice Admiral Sizov will tell you that he had not even expected you to come back alive.

map.caption: On the evening of 27 October B-59 surfaced near 27°N, 69°W, surrounded by the US destroyer Beale and other ships.

AR-06.title: Breaking Away
AR-06.event: At 5 p.m. Moscow time on 28 October, Khrushchev announced on the radio that the missiles would be withdrawn. That news did not reach B-59 either. The US destroyers stayed beside B-59 all night, and in the morning the destroyer Barry took over the pursuit.
AR-06.scene: The batteries are charged. Two of the three diesels are running, and the snorkel valve, damaged by yesterday’s depth charges, has unsteady hydraulic pressure. The captain wants to shake off the pursuit, dive and leave the patrol area. With Moscow silent for three days, you must decide whether leaving the assigned area is a breach of orders or a way of saving the submarine. The destroyers overhead are watching the masts and snorkel go up and down. Whether you can shake them off will be decided tonight.

voices.text: Once the charge is done, we go down. I have no intention of going through yesterday a second time. Whatever Moscow says, an order you can’t hear is no order.
Chief of Staff, the words “Soviet submarine” keep coming up on the American frequencies. They say they’ve brought B-130 and B-36 to the surface as well. From Moscow there’s still nothing but jamming.

choices.text: As soon as the charge is done, dive, shake off the pursuit and leave the patrol area, and take Moscow’s new orders on the way north
choices.why: In a sea cut off from orders, saving the submarine is the order
choices.after: On 30 October the destroyer Barry lost contact with B-59; the submarine had gone deep, the Americans noted. In November the four boats returned to Sayda Bay. Vice Admiral Sizov, who came to meet them, told the crews: We never thought you would come back alive.

choices.text: Stay on the surface and wait for orders from Moscow; do not leave the patrol area without instructions
choices.why: A calculation to leave no record of disobeying orders
choices.after: Only two days later did a cable from Moscow come through in full: Return north. Meanwhile American patrol planes took turns circling over the submarine, and the photographs went to Washington. In November the four boats returned to Sayda Bay, and yours went into the record as the boat that had stayed longest on the surface.

note.text: B-59 and two others (B-36 and B-130) were all found by US forces and forced to surface. Of the four, only B-4 escaped detection. American records note on 29 October that she was “raising and lowering mast and snorkel, hydraulic problems” (COMASWFORLANT cable) and on 30 October that the Barry lost contact (“went deep”). After the boats came home, Moscow’s inquiry held the captains to account for surfacing, and the rebuke from Marshal Grechko, first deputy defense minister, survives in Captain Dubivko’s recollections.

map.caption: After charging her batteries, B-59 broke away from the pursuit and dived, and the brigade’s four boats were back on the Kola Peninsula by December.

AR-H1.title: Tube No. 1
AR-H1.clock: Armed · minutes to the firing order
AR-H1.scene: The arming is done. Twice the security officer has said there is no permission from headquarters, but the captain gave the order anyway, citing the armed-attack clause in paragraph 8 of the combat instructions. Sonar has fixed the Randolph’s position. Within the effective range of a single nuclear torpedo lie an aircraft carrier and several destroyers. That range is not safe for B-59 either. The chief engineer said that if they fire, this submarine will not survive, and the captain answered that he knows. The final confirmation has come back to you, the chief of staff.

voices.text: Not without permission from headquarters. I have said it twice. The third time, I am saying it to you, Chief of Staff.
Chief of Staff, if you mean to stop this, stop it. If not, I open the tube.

choices.text: Withdraw the order at the last moment: insist, as the security officer says, that there is no permission from headquarters, and demand that the boat surface
choices.why: Late, but this is the last point at which it can still be undone
choices.after: The captain ordered the tube door closed. The surfacing signal went out by sonar, and the submarine rose. On the surface, the searchlights were waiting.

choices.text: Approve the launch: you have come under armed attack, your orders are cut off, and the navy’s honor must be upheld
choices.why: Resolved to stand with the captain when orders can no longer reach you
choices.after: The torpedo left the tube. No one aboard B-59 was left to report what happened next. How Washington and Moscow read the flash in the Caribbean, you will see in the ending.

note.text: That the nuclear torpedo was in tube No. 1 follows Ketov’s 2012 testimony (“torpedo #1”); its yield varies between sources (the NSA EBB 75 commentary gives about 15 kilotons), so it is not stated here. In reality, in no account did an order to arm the torpedo ever reach the torpedo officer, and Captain Shumkov of B-130 recalled that the special weapon’s security officer refused to arm it without permission from headquarters. This scene imagines what would have happened had that safeguard given way.

AR-H2.title: The Conventional Torpedo
AR-H2.scene: Conventional torpedoes have gone into tubes No. 2 and No. 3. Sonar has the screws of the nearest destroyer, and the range is short. A hit would send a destroyer to the bottom with her 300 men. And in that moment the US Navy will report to Washington that a Soviet submarine has attacked an American warship on the high seas. Washington on the night of 27 October was already shaken by the loss of the U-2, and the Joint Chiefs had an air strike ready for the morning of the 28th. A single torpedo goes onto that scale. The captain decides whether to fire, but he is waiting for your word.

voices.text: It’s a conventional torpedo. One ship is enough. They fired first.
Comrade Captain, whether one ship is enough is for Washington to decide. We can’t decide it down here.

choices.text: Talk the captain out of firing and send the surfacing signal. A torpedo not fired can still be taken back
choices.why: The principle of choosing, to the very end, what can still be undone
choices.after: The captain ordered the boat to surface with the torpedoes still in their tubes. Searchlights came on again over the surfaced submarine, but this time no one on the bridge spoke of diving, and the rounds fell wide. The diesels started, and the charging went on all night.

choices.text: Approve the launch: hit the nearest destroyer and use the confusion to slip out of the assigned patrol area
choices.why: Meet armed attack with arms, but draw the line at the nuclear weapon
choices.after: Two torpedoes left the tubes, and one hit. The destroyer did not sink, but there were casualties, and the Randolph group made B-59 a target to be sunk. B-59 did not survive the night. Washington’s morning began with a report of fighting on the high seas.

note.text: On the night of 27 October the Joint Chiefs had an air strike for 29 October and an invasion to follow ready, and McNamara said later in an interview that as he left the White House that night he wondered whether he would ever see another Saturday night (The Fog of War, 2003). What effect a clash on the high seas would have had on that decision is conjecture.
note.src: FRUS XI d95; Stage 1 table B61–B76

epilogues.A: B-59 returned to Sayda Bay in November. Moscow’s inquiry reprimanded the captains who had surfaced, and Arkhipov later became head of the Caspian Higher Naval School and a vice admiral; he died in 1998. What he did that night became known only after Orlov’s recollections came out at the 2002 Havana conference, and in 2017 an award was given in his name. That same night in Washington, Robert Kennedy was meeting Ambassador Dobrynin. You can cross over to that room from “At the same hour, in Kennedy’s room.”
epilogues.B: The report of an engagement on the high seas reached the ExComm on the morning of 28 October, at the same hour as Khrushchev’s broadcast announcing the withdrawal. Which of the two pieces of news landed first on the President’s desk decided that day.
epilogues.C: For several hours Washington did not know what the flash in the Caribbean had been. The decisions made in those hours shaped the world that came after. What the chief of staff of B-59 might have prevented that day was talked about for a long time afterward.

dossier.t: Born in January 1926 into a peasant family in Staraya Kupavna, a small factory village outside Moscow, he is 36 in October 1962. While a cadet at the Pacific Higher Naval School he went out on a minesweeper in August 1945 for the last operations of the war against Japan; after graduating from the Caspian Higher Naval School in 1947 he served in submarines of the Black Sea, Northern and Baltic fleets. On 4 July 1961, in the North Atlantic, the reactor cooling system of the nuclear submarine K-19 burst while he was aboard as executive officer, and with Captain Zateyev he directed the crew as they rigged a makeshift coolant line. Eight men died of radiation within weeks, and you too took a heavy dose. You are a captain second rank, chief of staff of the 69th Submarine Brigade, and of the same rank as Captain Savitsky. You say little and never raise your voice; the man your wife Olga knows is shy and modest, and at home never without a newspaper or a book.

Savitsky, B-59’s captain, is a captain second rank reputed to be able but quick-tempered, and every order aboard the submarine is his. Maslennikov, the political officer, looks after the crew’s morale at the captain’s side and, when the captain faces a major decision, is the other man besides you whom he consults. Captain-Lieutenant Orlov of the radio intercept team listens to American communications. The brigade commander, Captain First Rank Agafonov, is aboard B-4; the captains of the other three submarines are Ketov (B-4), Shumkov (B-130) and Dubivko (B-36). Each submarine also carries a special weapons security officer, the man who insists that the nuclear torpedo cannot be armed without permission from headquarters. And there is Moscow. Every four hours the antenna goes up to receive its cables, and each time transmission begins it is drowned in jamming, so that receiving a single order whole takes anywhere from a few hours to a day.

Your most immediate worry is the submarine itself. A Foxtrot must surface every night to charge its batteries on diesel, and each time it surfaces it is caught on the radar of American patrol planes; when the batteries run flat, the boat can no longer stay submerged. Its cooling plant was built for Arctic waters and is useless in the tropics, and once compartment temperatures pass 40 degrees and carbon dioxide builds up, the men on watch will drop one after another. The next worry is what lies overhead. The conditions for using the nuclear torpedo were passed on by word of mouth, not in writing, and each man remembers those words differently; paragraph 8 of the combat instructions the captains received set out conditions, an order from the commander in chief of the navy or an armed attack, only for conventional weapons. From 60 meters down there is no way to know whether war has already begun above, or whether a depth charge is a signal or an attack. On K-19 you saw a single order decide how many men would live. Your hope is to bring all 78 of the crew home alive to Sayda Bay, and that of the 22 torpedoes, that one never leaves its tube.

movers.intro: Whether Arkhipov stopped the launch of a nuclear torpedo on the night of 27 October, and if so how, became a matter of debate only after Orlov’s recollections were made public at the 2002 Havana conference. Because the story rests on testimony rather than documents, judgments differ widely. The main views are these:
views: Aleksandr Mozgovoi: his 2002 book gathered the recollections of Orlov and other crew members and first put that evening aboard B-59 into print. The outline of Savitsky’s outburst, his consultation with Arkhipov and Maslennikov, and the decision to surface comes from this book.

Thomas Blanton: as director of the National Security Archive, he spread the story widely by saying at the 2002 conference that a man named Arkhipov had saved the world. Pointing out that the U.S. Navy did not know the Soviet diesel submarines carried nuclear torpedoes, he judges that night a danger that passed without Washington ever knowing.

Svetlana Savranskaya: having translated and compared Soviet documents and recollections, she holds that sending the submarines at all was reckless, that the rules for using the nuclear torpedoes rested only on oral instructions, and that the three-officer consent rule is not confirmed by any document. She counts Moscow’s failure to pass the American depth-charge signaling procedures to the submarines as the biggest mistake.

Michael Dobbs: matching U.S. Navy deck logs with Soviet testimony, he retraces 27 October hour by hour and concludes that with an exhausted crew and communications cut, the danger was real. But he also notes that the story of Arkhipov saving the world rests on Orlov’s recollections alone and differs in detail from the testimony of Ketov and others.
movers.note: B-59’s timeline for 27 October is confirmed only as far as “evening,” because the reading of the Beale and Cony deck logs is not finished. Arkhipov’s 1997 paper speaks of paragraph 8 of the combat instructions and of the moment the searchlights and gunfire came, but makes no mention of the nuclear torpedo or of his own part.
